sources.source: Spark SQL Reference — EXPLAIN (Apache Spark documentation)

items.item: EXPLAIN EXTENDED names the four-stage pipeline: parsed, analyzed, optimized, physical
the parsed plan is unresolved, extracted from the query with no catalog lookup yet
analysis translates unresolved attributes and relations into fully typed, resolved objects
EXPLAIN FORMATTED generates a physical plan outline plus per-node detail

sources.source: Spark SQL Performance Tuning docs — spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (Apache Spark documentation)

items.item: the threshold configures the maximum broadcastable table size, default 10MB, and -1 disables broadcasting

at.step: Reveal: broadcast, no shuffle at all

sources.source: Spark SQL Reference — ANALYZE TABLE (Apache Spark documentation)

items.item: ANALYZE TABLE collects statistics the query optimizer uses to find a better execution plan, stored in the catalog

at.deep: Cost-based reordering, from real table statistics

items.item: The leading tick (') on an unresolved node is Catalyst's own textual convention in its tree-string representation (toString()), not a separate marker type — it appears on UnresolvedAttribute, UnresolvedRelation and any expression/operator still containing one, and disappears the instant analysis resolves every reference underneath it.

Subquery rewrites (named in the syllabus clause alongside pushdown and constant folding) are a separate optimizer rule family (e.g. decorrelating a correlated subquery into a join) not independently measured here — this topic's own examples.py covers the two simplest, most universally applicable rules (pushdown, folding) as representative, disclosing the rest as named only.

at.out: subquery rewrites named only in the syllabus mapping; not independently measured or sourced beyond the clause itself

items.item: Projection pushdown (reading only the columns a query actually needs from a columnar source) is the sibling rule to predicate pushdown this topic measures — both share the same motivation (do less work, as early as possible) but act on different parts of a plan; this topic's own measured example is predicate pushdown specifically.

BroadcastHashJoin's cost model compares the smaller side's estimated size (from the catalog, or a runtime size check for an already-materialized small relation) against spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold — not row count directly, which is why a differently-shaped small table could cross the threshold even with few rows if its rows are wide.

at.step: Reveal: broadcast, no shuffle at all

items.item: SortMergeJoin's own name describes its two-part mechanism directly: both shuffled sides are sorted by the join key before being merged in a single linear pass — the sort is why this strategy, unlike a hash join, tolerates a join key too large to fit in memory on either side.

A ShuffleHashJoin (distinct from both BroadcastHashJoin and SortMergeJoin) exists as a third strategy — shuffling both sides but skipping the sort, hash-probing instead — chosen when one shuffled side is still small enough to build an in-memory hash table from but too large to broadcast; named only, not independently measured, since forcing it reliably needs an explicit join hint this topic's own examples.py doesn't exercise.

at.out: ShuffleHashJoin named as the third strategy in the family; not independently measured

items.item: Cost-based join reordering (choosing which of several tables to join first in a multi-way join, not just which strategy to use for one join) requires spark.sql.cbo.enabled plus ANALYZE TABLE statistics on every table involved — a stricter requirement than strategy selection alone, which Catalyst does by default using size estimates even without ANALYZE TABLE having run.

at.deep: Cost-based reordering, from real table statistics

items.item: EXPLAIN FORMATTED's per-node 'Input' and 'Arguments' detail sections (not shown in this topic's own simpler string-matching measurements) are what an engineer actually reads line by line when diagnosing a specific operator's behaviour in production, beyond just confirming which stage produced which node.

AQE (disabled throughout this topic's own examples.py to keep Catalyst's up-front decisions legible) can override a join strategy Catalyst originally chose — specifically, converting an already-planned SortMergeJoin into a broadcast join at runtime if actual shuffle statistics turn out smaller than expected — the mirror case to this topic's own forced-SortMergeJoin demonstration, deferred to this chapter's own later AQE topic.

at.out: AQE's own runtime strategy conversion is this chapter's own later topic; named only as a methodology disclosure here

items.item: Constant folding and predicate pushdown both run inside the same named optimizer batch in Catalyst's rule executor (applied repeatedly until the plan stops changing, up to a fixed iteration limit) — this topic's two separate measured examples are two rules from that one pass, not two separate passes.

at.step: Reveal: constant folding, the same pass
